claim: Adjuvants can affect APCs function and boost adaptive immune responses post-vaccination.
source: Adjuvants can affect APCs function and boost adaptive immune responses post-vaccination.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific knowledge about adjuvants.

claim: The mechanisms by which adjuvants modulate the specificity of immune responses, particularly immunodominant epitope responses, and regulate antigen processing and presentation remain poorly defined.
source: However, whether they modulate the specificity of immune responses, particularly immunodominant epitope responses, and the mechanisms of regulating antigen processing and presentation remain poorly defined.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current knowledge, based on the authors' assessment of the literature.

claim: Adjuvants altered the antigen-specific CD4+ T-cell immunodominant epitope hierarchy in mice post-vaccination.
source: we screened the dominant epitopes of Th1 responses in mice post-vaccination with different adjuvants and found that the adjuvants altered the antigen-specific CD4+ T-cell immunodominant epitope hierarchy.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from screening overlapping synthetic peptides in vaccinated mice.

claim: The peptide repertoires presented by APCs were significantly altered by the adjuvants.
source: MHC-II immunopeptidomes demonstrated that the peptide repertoires presented by APCs were significantly altered by the adjuvants.
evidence: This is supported by MHC-II immunopeptidome analysis data.

claim: No novel peptide presentation was detected after adjuvant treatment.
source: Unexpectedly, no novel peptide presentation was detected after adjuvant treatment, whereas peptides with high binding stability for MHC-II presented in the control group were missing after adjuvant stimulation, particularly in the MPLA- and CpG-stimulated groups.
evidence: This finding is based on immunopeptidome data comparing adjuvant-treated and control groups.

claim: Peptides with high binding stability for MHC-II presented in the control group were missing after adjuvant stimulation, particularly in the MPLA- and CpG-stimulated groups.
source: Unexpectedly, no novel peptide presentation was detected after adjuvant treatment, whereas peptides with high binding stability for MHC-II presented in the control group were missing after adjuvant stimulation, particularly in the MPLA- and CpG-stimulated groups.
evidence: This is supported by immunopeptidome data and MHC-II binding stability predictions.

claim: The low-stability peptide present in the adjuvant groups effectively elicited robust T-cell responses and formed immune memory.
source: The low-stability peptide present in the adjuvant groups effectively elicited robust T-cell responses and formed immune memory.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from ELISpot assays and flow cytometry at different time points post-immunization.

claim: Adjuvants (MPLA and CpG) inhibit high-stability peptide presentation instead of revealing cryptic epitopes.
source: Collectively, our results suggest that adjuvants (MPLA and CpG) inhibit high-stability peptide presentation instead of revealing cryptic epitopes, which may alter the specificity of CD4+ T-cell-dominant epitope responses.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the immunopeptidome and T-cell response data.

claim: The capacity of adjuvants to modify peptide–MHC (pMHC) stability and antigen-specific T-cell immunodominant epitope responses has fundamental implications for the selection of suitable adjuvants in the vaccine design process and epitope vaccine development.
source: The capacity of adjuvants to modify peptide–MHC (pMHC) stability and antigen-specific T-cell immunodominant epitope responses has fundamental implications for the selection of suitable adjuvants in the vaccine design process and epitope vaccine development.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the implications of the findings for vaccine development.

claim: The most commonly used adjuvants stimulate antibody responses by relying on B-cells.
source: The most commonly used adjuvants stimulate antibody responses by relying on B-cells (Levast et al., 2014; Petrovsky, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: B-cell priming and memory forming are dependent on the cognate help of antigen-specific T-cells.
source: B-cell priming and memory forming are dependent on the cognate help of antigen-specific T-cells.
evidence: This is based on established immunological knowledge.

claim: T-cells have direct effector functions against pathogenic infections.
source: T-cells also have direct effector functions against pathogenic infections.
evidence: This is based on established immunological knowledge.

claim: Antigen-specific T-cells play a vital role in shaping the immune response during vaccination.
source: Thus, antigen-specific T-cells play a vital role in shaping the immune response during vaccination.
evidence: This is an inference based on the roles of T-cells described previously.

claim: The mechanisms by which adjuvants regulate the specificity of antigen-specific T-cell responses remain poorly understood.
source: However, the mechanisms by which adjuvants regulate the specificity of antigen-specific T-cell responses remain poorly understood.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Antigen-specific T-cell responses mainly focus on several peptides derived from antigen amino acids called immunodominant epitopes.
source: Antigen-specific T-cell responses mainly focus on several peptides derived from antigen amino acids called immunodominant epitopes (Sant et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Although specific T-cell responses are provoked by the same antigen, their response epitopes may differ, leading to diverse effects.
source: Although specific T-cell responses are provoked by the same antigen, their response epitopes may differ, leading to diverse effects.
evidence: This is based on immunological knowledge and inference.

claim: Peptides presented by antigen-presenting cells (APCs) provide the first major signal for T-cells priming and determining their specificity.
source: Peptides presented by antigen-presenting cells (APCs) provide the first major signal for T-cells priming and determining their specificity.
evidence: This is based on established immunological knowledge.

claim: Adjuvants can activate APCs and increase the expression of co-stimulatory molecules of APCs.
source: Although adjuvants can activate APCs and increase the expression of co-stimulatory molecules of APCs (Pulendran, 2004), the effect of adjuvants on the peptide repertoires presented by APCs or modulation of epitope-specific T-cell responses remains unknown.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The effect of adjuvants on the peptide repertoires presented by APCs or modulation of epitope-specific T-cell responses remains unknown.
source: Although adjuvants can activate APCs and increase the expression of co-stimulatory molecules of APCs (Pulendran, 2004), the effect of adjuvants on the peptide repertoires presented by APCs or modulation of epitope-specific T-cell responses remains unknown.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Helicobacter pylori infects more than half the global population.
source: Helicobacter pylori infects more than half the global population and causes chronic gastritis, peptic ulcers, gastric mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma (MALT), and gastric cancer (Malfertheiner et al., 2023; Moss et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Helicobacter pylori causes chronic gastritis, peptic ulcers, gastric mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma (MALT), and gastric cancer.
source: Helicobacter pylori infects more than half the global population and causes chronic gastritis, peptic ulcers, gastric mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma (MALT), and gastric cancer (Malfertheiner et al., 2023; Moss et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Studies in human and mouse models showed that the Th1 response provides more important protection against H. pylori than a humoral immune response.
source: Studies in human and mouse models showed that the Th1 response provides more important protection against H. pylori than a humoral immune response.
evidence: This is based on previous studies, though not explicitly cited in this sentence.

claim: No effective vaccines have been developed to drive T-cell responses against H. pylori.
source: Unfortunately, no effective vaccines have been developed to drive T-cell responses (Friedrich and Gerhard, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: H. pylori provides an ideal experimental model to determine the mechanisms by which adjuvants regulate T-cell responses.
source: H. pylori provides an ideal experimental model to determine the mechanisms by which adjuvants regulate T-cell responses.
evidence: This is an inference based on the characteristics of H. pylori infection and immune responses.

claim: Some pattern recognition receptor (PRR) ligand adjuvants can induce a strong T-cell response.
source: Studies on widely used adjuvants have found that some pattern recognition receptor (PRR) ligand adjuvants can induce a strong T-cell response (Li et al., 2022; Tom et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PRR ligand adjuvants that target PRRs on the surface of innate immune cells promote cytokine secretion and upregulate co-stimulatory molecule expression.
source: PRR ligand adjuvants that target PRRs on the surface of innate immune cells, such as macrophages and dendritic cells, promote cytokine secretion and upregulate co-stimulatory molecule expression (Didierlaurent et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Typical PRR adjuvants include MPLA, CpG, and MDP.
source: Typical PRR adjuvants include MPLA, CpG, and MDP, which induce effective T-cell responses and have been successfully used in many vaccines such as HPV, HSV, and COVID-19 vaccines (Fan et al., 2022; Del Giudice et al., 2018; Iwicka et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: MPLA, CpG, and MDP induce effective T-cell responses and have been successfully used in many vaccines such as HPV, HSV, and COVID-19 vaccines.
source: Typical PRR adjuvants include MPLA, CpG, and MDP, which induce effective T-cell responses and have been successfully used in many vaccines such as HPV, HSV, and COVID-19 vaccines (Fan et al., 2022; Del Giudice et al., 2018; Iwicka et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The impact of MPLA, CpG, and MDP on antigen processing and presentation on APCs and immunodominant epitope responses is unknown.
source: However, their impact on antigen processing and presentation on APCs and immunodominant epitope responses is unknown.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Immunodominant epitopes recognized by antigen-specific T-cells were altered by adjuvants.
source: In this study, using MPLA, CpG, and MDP adjuvants and H. pylori antigens, we demonstrated that immunodominant epitopes recognized by antigen-specific T-cells were altered by adjuvants.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The adjuvants MPLA and CpG modulate the peptide repertoires present on the APCs surface.
source: Furthermore, we showed that the adjuvants MPLA and CpG modulate the peptide repertoires present on the APCs surface.
evidence: This is supported by immunopeptidome data from the study.

claim: Instead of revealing cryptic epitopes or presenting high-stability peptides, peptides with high binding stability for MHC-II were restrained, and low-stability peptides were presented by APCs after adjuvant treatment.
source: Surprisingly, instead of revealing cryptic epitopes or presenting high-stability peptides, peptides with high binding stability for MHC-II were restrained, and low-stability peptides were presented by APCs after adjuvant treatment.
evidence: This is supported by immunopeptidome data and MHC-II binding predictions.

claim: The low-stability peptide presented in the adjuvant groups effectively elicits a T-cell response.
source: The low-stability peptide presented in the adjuvant groups effectively elicits a T-cell response.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from T-cell response assays.

claim: Altering pMHC stability in APCs provides a fundamentally new mechanism for PRR adjuvants to regulate adaptive immunity.
source: Thus, altering pMHC stability in APCs provides a fundamentally new mechanism for PRR adjuvants to regulate adaptive immunity.
evidence: This is an interpretation and inference based on the study's findings.

claim: T-cells from the CpG group exhibited a dominant response to 18mer peptides U313–330 and U403–426.
source: T-cells from the CpG group exhibited a dominant response to 18mer peptides U313–330 and U403–426, while T-cells from the MDP group exhibited a dominant response to U409–426 and U481–498.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: T-cells from the MDP group exhibited a dominant response to U409–426 and U481–498.
source: T-cells from the CpG group exhibited a dominant response to 18mer peptides U313–330 and U403–426, while T-cells from the MDP group exhibited a dominant response to U409–426 and U481–498.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: T-cells from the MPLA group primarily recognized U313–U330 and U505–522.
source: T-cells from the MPLA group primarily recognized U313–U330 and U505–522, whereas U481–U504 was the dominant region in T-cells from the no-adjuvant group (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: U481–U504 was the dominant region in T-cells from the no-adjuvant group.
source: T-cells from the MPLA group primarily recognized U313–U330 and U505–522, whereas U481–U504 was the dominant region in T-cells from the no-adjuvant group (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Immunodominant epitopes responding to antigen-specific T-cells varied in different adjuvant vaccination groups.
source: These data indicate that immunodominant epitopes responding to antigen-specific T-cells varied in different adjuvant vaccination groups.
evidence: This is an inference based on the flow cytometry data from Figure 1.

claim: T-cell repertoires are the same in naïve mice.
source: Considering that T-cell repertoires are the same in naïve mice, we speculate that dominant epitope variations in different adjuvant vaccination groups result from alterations in APCs peptide presentation.
evidence: This is based on immunological knowledge about naïve mice.

claim: Dominant epitope variations in different adjuvant vaccination groups result from alterations in APCs peptide presentation.
source: Considering that T-cell repertoires are the same in naïve mice, we speculate that dominant epitope variations in different adjuvant vaccination groups result from alterations in APCs peptide presentation.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed data and immunological reasoning.

claim: A total of 4074 peptides were identified across all groups.
source: A total of 4074 peptides were identified: 3408, 3257, 3227, and 3330 peptides in the PBS, MDP, MPLA, and CpG groups, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 3408 peptides were identified in the PBS group.
source: A total of 4074 peptides were identified: 3408, 3257, 3227, and 3330 peptides in the PBS, MDP, MPLA, and CpG groups, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 3257 peptides were identified in the MDP group.
source: A total of 4074 peptides were identified: 3408, 3257, 3227, and 3330 peptides in the PBS, MDP, MPLA, and CpG groups, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 3227 peptides were identified in the MPLA group.
source: A total of 4074 peptides were identified: 3408, 3257, 3227, and 3330 peptides in the PBS, MDP, MPLA, and CpG groups, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 3330 peptides were identified in the CpG group.
source: A total of 4074 peptides were identified: 3408, 3257, 3227, and 3330 peptides in the PBS, MDP, MPLA, and CpG groups, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The number and length distributions of the peptides were not influenced by the adjuvants.
source: As expected, the number and length distributions of the peptides were not influenced by the adjuvants (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Most identified peptides were 16 mer.
source: Most identified peptides were 16 mer.
evidence: This is supported by the length distribution data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: No obvious differences in binding motifs were observed following the adjuvant treatment.
source: Next, the binding motifs of all identified peptides were analyzed (Figure 2D). No obvious differences were observed following the adjuvant treatment.
evidence: This is supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: No major differences in binding motifs per individual MHC-II allele were detected.
source: The binding motifs of the peptides per individual MHC-II allele, H2-IA, and H2-IE, were also analyzed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). No major differences were detected.
evidence: This is supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The amino acids observed at the main anchor locations were consistent with the expected binding motifs.
source: The amino acids observed at the main anchor locations were consistent with the expected binding motifs.
evidence: This is based on comparison with known MHC-II binding motifs.

claim: Most MS-detected peptides bind to MHC-II alleles (% rank <10) and are generally assigned to the H2-IA allele.
source: The binding affinity data predicted using NetMHCIIpan showed that most MS-detected peptides bind to MHC-II alleles (% rank <10) and are generally assigned to the H2-IA allele (Figure 2E; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by binding prediction data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Adjuvants did not affect MHC-II binding characteristics.
source: These results indicate that adjuvants did not affect MHC-II binding characteristics.
evidence: This is an inference based on the motif and binding affinity data.

claim: Fewer than 350 peptides were observed in J774A.1 cells at a peptide spectrum match (PSM) level of <1.0% false discovery rate (FDR).
source: Briefly, 5×108 J774A.1 cells were used for immunopeptidomics. Moreover, fewer than 350 peptides were observed at a peptide spectrum match (PSM) level of <1.0% false discovery rate (FDR).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: More than 5500 peptides were detected in 108 A20 cells at FDR <1.0%.
source: However, more than 5500 peptides were detected in 108 A20 cells at FDR <1.0% (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: CD86 and MHC-II molecule expression on J774A.1 cell was substantially lower than that on A20 cells.
source: CD86 and MHC-II molecule expression on J774A.1 cell was substantially lower than that on A20 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Low MHC-II expression on J774A.1 cell could be the reason for the lack of peptides identified by LC–MS/MS.
source: Low MHC-II expression on J774A.1 cell could be the reason for the lack of peptides identified by LC–MS/MS.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between MHC-II expression and peptide identification.

claim: A20 cells instead of J774A.1 cells were used for the subsequent experiments.
source: Thus, A20 cells instead of J774A.1 cells were used for the subsequent experiments.
evidence: This is a methodological decision based on the comparative data.

claim: H. pylori contained more than 3000 proteins, but less than 30 proteins were detected in the MHC-II immunopeptidomes.
source: Surprisingly, H. pylori contained more than 3000 proteins, but less than 30 proteins were detected in the MHC-II immunopeptidomes (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by immunopeptidome data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The abundance of MHC-IP-identified proteins in the entire H. pylori proteome MS data was similar to that of other bacterial proteins.
source: The abundance of MHC-IP-identified proteins in the entire H. pylori proteome MS data was analyzed, and we found that the abundance of these proteins was similar to that of other bacterial proteins (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by proteome abundance data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: MHC-IP proteins contained more presentable peptides than most other bacterial proteins.
source: MHC-IP proteins contained more presentable peptides than most other bacterial proteins (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by MHC-II presentation potential analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: 82.4% host MHC-II peptides were present in all the groups.
source: By analyzing the host and exogenous MHC-II peptides present in different adjuvant groups, we found that 82.4% host MHC-II peptides were present in all the groups; however, only 34.4% exogenous MHC-II peptides were conserved after adjuvant treatment (Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunopeptidome data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only 34.4% exogenous MHC-II peptides were conserved after adjuvant treatment.
source: By analyzing the host and exogenous MHC-II peptides present in different adjuvant groups, we found that 82.4% host MHC-II peptides were present in all the groups; however, only 34.4% exogenous MHC-II peptides were conserved after adjuvant treatment (Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunopeptidome data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Adjuvants affect exogenous peptide presentation.
source: These data indicate that adjuvants affect exogenous peptide presentation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential conservation of exogenous vs. host peptides.

claim: Many exogenous peptides are missing after adjuvant MPLA or CpG treatment.
source: Many exogenous peptides are missing after adjuvant MPLA or CpG treatment.
evidence: This is supported by immunopeptidome data.

claim: No changes were detected in the number of peptides in the host.
source: However, no changes were detected in the number of peptides in the host (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by immunopeptidome data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The repertoires of exogenous peptides presented by APCs are affected exclusively by adjuvants, and a smaller number of peptides are present.
source: These data indicate that the repertoires of exogenous peptides presented by APCs are affected exclusively by adjuvants, and a smaller number of peptides are present.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects on exogenous vs. host peptides.

claim: A strong correlation between the bacterial protein abundances in different adjuvant-treated groups was observed.
source: We observed a strong correlation between the bacterial protein abundances in different adjuvant-treated groups (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by proteome data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The bacterial protein abundance in the immunopeptidome changed significantly among the adjuvant-treated groups.
source: We then compared the abundance of bacterial proteins in the proteome and MHC-II immunopeptidomes and found that the bacterial protein abundance in the immunopeptidome changed significantly among the adjuvant-treated groups, and no peptides of several bacterial antigens were detected in some groups.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Only several proteins showed altered abundance in the proteome.
source: However, only several proteins showed altered abundance in the proteome (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by proteome data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The changes in exogenous peptide presentation among the adjuvant groups cannot be explained by antigen phagocytosis.
source: These results suggest that the changes in exogenous peptide presentation among the adjuvant groups cannot be explained by antigen phagocytosis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proteome and immunopeptidome comparison.

claim: The overall abundance of bacterial proteins in the APCs proteome was low.
source: The overall abundance of bacterial proteins in the APCs proteome was low (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by proteome data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Individual bacterial protein expression was below that of most host proteins in both the PBS- and adjuvant-treated groups.
source: Individual bacterial protein expression was below that of most host proteins in both the PBS- and adjuvant-treated groups (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by proteome data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The intensities of bacterial MHC-II peptides were similar to those of peptides from the host in the PBS-treated group according to the immunopeptidome data.
source: In contrast to the low abundance of bacterial proteins, the intensities of their MHC-II peptides were similar to those of peptides from the host in the PBS-treated group according to the immunopeptidome data (Figure 5B), indicating that bacterial peptides are preferentially present.
evidence: This is supported by immunopeptidome data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Bacterial peptides are preferentially present in the PBS-treated group.
source: In contrast to the low abundance of bacterial proteins, the intensities of their MHC-II peptides were similar to those of peptides from the host in the PBS-treated group according to the immunopeptidome data (Figure 5B), indicating that bacterial peptides are preferentially present.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of bacterial protein abundance and peptide intensities.

claim: In the MPLA- and CpG-treated groups, the intensities of bacterial MHC-II peptides in the immunopeptidome were much lower than those in the hosts.
source: However, in the MPLA- and CpG-treated groups, the intensities of bacterial MHC-II peptides in the immunopeptidome were much lower than those in the hosts (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by immunopeptidome data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Adjuvants MPLA and CpG restrain bacterial peptide presentation.
source: These results indicate that adjuvants MPLA and CpG restrain bacterial peptide presentation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the immunopeptidome data.

claim: Many proteins involved in antigen processing, peptidase function, ubiquitination pathways, and IFN signaling were altered after adjuvant treatment, particularly in the MPLA- and CpG-treated groups.
source: Through KEGG enrichment analysis, we found that many proteins involved in antigen processing, peptidase function, ubiquitination pathways, and IFN signaling were altered after adjuvant treatment, particularly in the MPLA- and CpG-treated groups (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by proteome data and KEGG enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: MPLA and CpG adjuvants may affect the antigen processing of APCs, resulting in fewer peptide presentations.
source: These data suggest that MPLA and CpG adjuvants may affect the antigen processing of APCs, resulting in fewer peptide presentations.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the proteome data showing altered expression of antigen processing proteins.

claim: The number of peptides from the exogenous antigens was significantly reduced in the MPLA- and CpG-treated groups.
source: We confirmed that the number of peptides from the exogenous antigens was significantly reduced in the MPLA- and CpG-treated groups.
evidence: This is supported by immunopeptidome data.

claim: The IC50 of the peptides binding to H2-IA and H2-IE alleles in the CpG- or MPLA-treated groups were much higher than those of the deficient peptides in the corresponding groups.
source: Compared to that in the PBS-treated group, the IC50 of the peptides binding to H2-IA and H2-IE alleles in the CpG- or MPLA-treated groups were much higher than those of the deficient peptides in the corresponding groups, which indicated that the peptides presented in the MPLA- and CpG-treated groups have lower binding stability for MHC-II (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by MHC-II binding prediction data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The peptides presented in the MPLA- and CpG-treated groups have lower binding stability for MHC-II.
source: Compared to that in the PBS-treated group, the IC50 of the peptides binding to H2-IA and H2-IE alleles in the CpG- or MPLA-treated groups were much higher than those of the deficient peptides in the corresponding groups, which indicated that the peptides presented in the MPLA- and CpG-treated groups have lower binding stability for MHC-II (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is an inference based on IC50 values.

claim: The peptides present in both adjuvant- and PBS-treated control groups were mainly derived from proteins tuf, recA, etc.
source: Furthermore, we found that the peptides present in both adjuvant- and PBS-treated control groups were mainly derived from proteins tuf, recA, etc., and the deficient peptides in the MPLA- or CpG-treated group were mainly derived from proteins such as ureA and hopZ (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by immunopeptidome data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The deficient peptides in the MPLA- or CpG-treated group were mainly derived from proteins such as ureA and hopZ.
source: Furthermore, we found that the peptides present in both adjuvant- and PBS-treated control groups were mainly derived from proteins tuf, recA, etc., and the deficient peptides in the MPLA- or CpG-treated group were mainly derived from proteins such as ureA and hopZ (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by immunopeptidome data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Strong correlations between fragment ions and retention times were observed for synthetic peptides and experimental spectra.
source: The tandem mass spectra of the synthetic peptides and experimental spectra were compared, and strong correlations between fragment ions and retention times were observed (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by MS/MS data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The peptides missing in the MPLA-/CpG-treated groups had better binding stability for MHC-II molecules than the peptides presented in the adjuvant-treated groups.
source: We confirmed that the peptides missing in the MPLA-/CpG-treated groups had better binding stability for MHC-II molecules than the peptides presented in the adjuvant-treated groups (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by MHC-II competition-binding assay data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Epitopes with high binding stability were deficient after MPLA and CpG treatment.
source: These data indicate that epitopes with high binding stability were deficient after MPLA and CpG treatment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the binding stability data.

claim: Positive responses to the low-stability peptides recA #23 and NCTC11637-00693 #38 as well as highly stable peptides ureA #2, ureA #3, and hopZ #53 were found on day 10.
source: We found positive responses to the low-stability peptides recA #23 (AFIDAEHALDVHYAKR) and NCTC11637-00693 #38 (IHSQVEANTQAQEGLR) as well as highly stable peptides ureA #2 (ASMIHEVGIEAMFPDGTK), ureA #3(YVEAVALISAHIMEEAR), and hopZ #53(KMLELANQIKTNLSAIPQ) on day 10 (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by ELISpot data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: On day 28, the response to the low-stability peptide recA #23 was not weaker than that of the other peptides.
source: On day 28, the response to the low-stability peptide recA #23 (AFIDAEHALDVHYAKR) was not weaker than that of the other peptides (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by ELISpot data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Peptides with low MHC-II stability skew T-cell repertoires toward high-affinity clonotypes that have excellent responses against pathogen infection.
source: Peptides with low MHC-II stability skew T-cell repertoires toward high-affinity clonotypes that have excellent responses against pathogen infection (Baumgartner et al., 2010; Busch and Pamer, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The low-stability peptide recA #23 induced more robust CD4+ T-cell responses at lower peptide concentrations.
source: We found that the low-stability peptide recA #23 induced more robust CD4+ T-cell responses at lower peptide concentrations (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The low-stability peptide presented in the adjuvant-treated groups could induce robust CD4+ T-cell responses effectively.
source: These data suggest that the low-stability peptide presented in the adjuvant-treated groups could induce robust CD4+ T-cell responses effectively.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ELISpot and flow cytometry data.

claim: Adjuvants alter the specificity of the dominant Th1 epitope responses post-vaccination.
source: We demonstrated that adjuvants alter the specificity of the dominant Th1 epitope responses post-vaccination.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: The peptide motifs binding to MHC-II were generally consistent following stimulation with adjuvants.
source: The peptide motifs binding to MHC-II were generally consistent following stimulation with adjuvants.
evidence: This is based on motif analysis data.

claim: The exogenous peptide repertoires of APCs changed following adjuvant stimulation.
source: However, the exogenous peptide repertoires of APCs changed.
evidence: This is based on immunopeptidome data.

claim: Low- and high-stability peptides were presented by APCs in the control group.
source: Low- and high-stability peptides were presented by APCs in the control group; however, fewer peptides were detected in the adjuvant groups, and peptides with high binding stability for MHC-II presented in the control group were missing after adjuvant stimulation, particularly in the CpG group.
